title: hx-indicator: Declarative Loading States via .htmx-request CSS Classes

progressiveExplaining.eli5: When you click a button to download a file, you want a spinning wheel to appear so you know the computer is working. `hx-indicator` points to any spinner or loading message. While the request is traveling across the internet, HTMX automatically shows the spinner and hides it as soon as the answer arrives.
progressiveExplaining.junior: `hx-indicator` points to an element that will be shown while an HTMX request is in flight: `<button hx-get="/data" hx-indicator="#spinner">Load</button>`. HTMX automatically adds the `.htmx-request` CSS class to the indicator element (and the triggering element) during the request, and removes it upon completion. The default HTMX stylesheet automatically hides `.htmx-indicator` (`opacity: 0`) and shows it when `.htmx-request` is added (`opacity: 1`).
progressiveExplaining.senior: Architecturally, `hx-indicator` provides zero-JavaScript loading state management. Instead of creating imperative boolean state variables (`isLoading = true`) and manual cleanup try/finally blocks, HTMX manages state directly in the DOM class list. You can target closest indicators (`hx-indicator="closest tr"`), style buttons into disabled/busy states (`button.htmx-request { pointer-events: none; opacity: 0.6; }`), and create smooth CSS opacity transitions.
progressiveExplaining.underTheHood: When an AJAX request begins (`issueAjaxRequest`), HTMX resolves the indicator target element. It adds the `htmx-request` class to the indicator DOM token list. It tracks active requests in a request queue. When the request resolves (`xhr.onloadend` or `fetch.finally`), HTMX removes the `htmx-request` class from the indicator element and dispatches `htmx:afterRequest`.

codeComparison.title: Manual Loading State Boilerplate vs Declarative hx-indicator
codeComparison.summary: Manual spinner toggling requires try/finally blocks in JS; `hx-indicator` coordinates loading visibility through CSS classes.

legacyOrBad.label: Manual JS Spinner Toggling
legacyOrBad.snippet: spinner.style.display = 'block'; try { await fetch(); } finally { spinner.style.display = 'none'; } // ❌ Manual

modernOrGood.label: Declarative hx-indicator with CSS
modernOrGood.snippet: <button hx-post="/save" hx-indicator="#spinner">Save</button> // ✅ NEW: Zero JS needed

interviewGotchas.question: What happens if an element has `class="htmx-indicator"` but no `hx-indicator` attribute is defined on the button?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: Interviewers test your knowledge of default indicator scoping.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: If no `hx-indicator` attribute is explicitly provided on the triggering element, HTMX looks for any child element matching `.htmx-indicator` *inside* the triggering element and adds `.htmx-request` to the triggering element itself. If the indicator is located outside the element, `hx-indicator="#my-spinner"` must be explicitly specified.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: Placing `.htmx-indicator` on a sibling element without specifying `hx-indicator` will result in the spinner never appearing.

interviewGotchas.question: Can `hx-indicator` use relative directional selectors like `closest`?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: Checks precision regarding relative selector resolution in indicator attributes.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: Yes. `hx-indicator` supports the same relative selectors as `hx-target`: `hx-indicator="closest tr"`, `hx-indicator="find .spinner"`, `hx-indicator="next .loading-bar"`, or `hx-indicator="this"`.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: Using `hx-indicator="closest .row"` adds the `.htmx-request` class to the entire row, allowing you to dim the whole table row with CSS during updates.
